title: Women's Health & Obstetrics
summary: How the female reproductive system works, what goes wrong with it, and what pregnancy does to every other organ. Built around the can't-miss diagnoses and the first action for each.

lessons.title: Taking the history and doing the pelvic exam
lessons.body:
## Why the history carries most of the weight

The pelvic organs sit deep inside the body. You cannot see or feel most of what goes wrong with them, so the story a patient tells does more diagnostic work here than in almost any other body system. A well-taken gynecologic history narrows a huge differential before a glove comes out of the box.

### The four histories you always take

**Menstrual.** Age at first period (menarche, usually `12-13`), date of the last menstrual period (LMP), cycle length counted from day 1 to day 1 (normal `24-38` days), days of flow (normal `<= 8`), and how heavy. Heavy is measured in soaked pads or tampons per hour and in clots bigger than a quarter, not in adjectives.

**Obstetric.** Every pregnancy and how it ended. This is written in shorthand called **GTPAL**: Gravida (total pregnancies), Term (deliveries at `>= 37` weeks), Preterm (`20` to `36 6/7` weeks), Abortions (losses before `20` weeks, spontaneous or induced), Living children. A patient who has had three pregnancies, one full-term baby, one loss at 10 weeks, and is pregnant now is `G3 T1 P0 A1 L1`. Twins count as one pregnancy but two living children.

**Sexual.** Ask about partners, practices, protection, past infections, and pregnancy intention. Ask everyone, in the same neutral voice, and use the patient's words for their partners and their body.

**Screening.** Last cervical cancer screening and result, last mammogram, HPV vaccination.

> **Key:** In anyone with a uterus between roughly `11` and `55` with abdominal pain, dizziness, or bleeding, the history is not complete until a pregnancy test is ordered. Patients are sometimes wrong about whether they could be pregnant.

### The exam, step by step

1. Explain what you will do and why, and get spoken permission before each part.
2. Offer a chaperone and document it. In most systems a chaperone is offered for every sensitive exam regardless of the clinician's gender.
3. Empty bladder, drape, patient's choice of position, head of bed up so you can see each other's faces.
4. **External inspection**: skin, hair distribution, lesions, discharge, signs of trauma.
5. **Speculum**: warmed, lubricated, inserted at a downward angle following the natural slope of the canal. Look at the cervix and the walls. This is when you collect samples: cervical cytology, nucleic acid testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia, and vaginal fluid for a wet mount (saline and potassium hydroxide slides) and pH.
6. **Bimanual**: two gloved fingers inside, the other hand on the lower abdomen. You are feeling uterine size, position, and tenderness, then each adnexa for a mass. Pain when the cervix is moved (cervical motion tenderness) points toward pelvic infection.
7. Offer tissue and privacy to dress before you discuss anything.

> **On shift:** Nothing in the exam has to happen all at once. A patient can say stop at any point, and stopping is a finding, not a failure.

### When the exam is not needed

A pelvic exam is not required to prescribe most contraception, and it is not required for routine screening in an asymptomatic patient under `21`. Self-collected or clinician-collected swabs diagnose most vaginitis and most sexually transmitted infections without a speculum.

> **Trap:** A normal pelvic exam never rules out pregnancy, and it never rules out an ectopic. Only the pregnancy test and imaging do that.
keyPoints: GTPAL: Gravida, Term (>= 37 wk), Preterm (20-36 6/7), Abortions (< 20 wk), Living.
Pregnancy test before almost any gynecologic or abdominal workup in a person of reproductive age.
Offer a chaperone every time, get permission before each step, and stop when asked.
Speculum first (samples, cervix), bimanual second (size, masses, cervical motion tenderness).
No pelvic exam is needed to start most contraception or to screen an asymptomatic patient under 21.

checks.q: A patient has been pregnant four times: two babies born at 39 weeks, one born at 33 weeks, one miscarriage at 9 weeks. All three babies are alive. What is her GTPAL?
checks.why: Four pregnancies (G4), two at or past 37 weeks (T2), one between 20 and 36 6/7 weeks (P1), one loss before 20 weeks (A1), three living children (L3).

checks.q: Which finding on bimanual exam most suggests pelvic infection?
choices: Pain when the cervix is moved side to side
A smooth cervix with clear mucus
checks.why: Cervical motion tenderness reflects peritoneal irritation around the tubes and is a classic pelvic inflammatory disease sign. The other findings are normal.

checks.q: A 19-year-old with no symptoms wants to start combined oral contraceptive pills. What does she need first?
choices: A speculum exam and cervical cytology
A bimanual exam to size the uterus
Blood pressure and a focused medical history
checks.why: Starting hormonal contraception needs a blood pressure and a history screening for contraindications. A pelvic exam is not required, and cytology does not start until age 21.

lessons.title: Menstrual disorders: absent, heavy, and painful periods
lessons.body:
## The cycle in one paragraph

The brain's pituitary releases follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which ripens a follicle in the ovary. That follicle makes estrogen, which thickens the uterine lining. A surge of luteinizing hormone (LH) around day 14 releases the egg (ovulation). The leftover follicle, now called the corpus luteum, makes progesterone, which stabilizes the lining. If no pregnancy implants, the corpus luteum dies at about day 28, progesterone falls, and the lining sheds. Every menstrual problem below is a break somewhere in that loop.

### No periods (amenorrhea)

**Primary** amenorrhea means no period ever, by `15` with normal breast development, or by `13` with none. Causes: chromosomal (Turner syndrome), structural (imperforate hymen, absent uterus), or pituitary.

**Secondary** amenorrhea means periods stopped for `3` months (or `6` months if cycles were irregular). The workup order never changes:

1. **Pregnancy test.** Always. It is the most common cause by far.
2. **TSH** and **prolactin**. Thyroid disease and a prolactin-secreting pituitary tumor both silence the cycle and both are treatable.
3. **FSH**. High FSH means the ovary has stopped responding (primary ovarian insufficiency or menopause). Low or normal FSH points upstream to the brain, often from low body weight, heavy exercise, or stress (functional hypothalamic amenorrhea).

> **Key:** Pregnancy test, then TSH and prolactin, then FSH. Ordering an expensive hormone panel before the urine pregnancy test is the classic exam mistake.

### Heavy or irregular bleeding (abnormal uterine bleeding, AUB)

The organizing framework is **PALM-COEIN**. PALM causes are structural and you can see them: **P**olyp, **A**denomyosis, **L**eiomyoma (fibroid), **M**alignancy. COEIN causes are not structural: **C**oagulopathy, **O**vulatory dysfunction, **E**ndometrial, **I**atrogenic, **N**ot otherwise classified.

**Fibroids (leiomyomas)** are benign smooth-muscle tumors, extremely common, and cause heavy bleeding, bulk pressure, and an enlarged irregular uterus. **Adenomyosis** is endometrial tissue inside the uterine muscle, giving a boggy, tender, uniformly enlarged uterus.

> **Trap:** Any bleeding after menopause is cancer until proven otherwise and needs endometrial sampling, not reassurance.

### Painful periods (dysmenorrhea)

**Primary** dysmenorrhea is pain from prostaglandin-driven uterine cramping with no underlying disease. It starts within a couple of years of menarche and responds to NSAIDs started `1-2` days before flow, plus hormonal contraception.

**Secondary** dysmenorrhea has a cause. The big one is **endometriosis**: uterine lining tissue growing outside the uterus, which bleeds each cycle into places with no exit. Triad is painful periods, pain with sex (dyspareunia), and infertility. Definitive diagnosis is laparoscopy, but treatment usually starts empirically with NSAIDs and hormones.

### PCOS

Polycystic ovary syndrome is diagnosed by **Rotterdam criteria**: any `2` of `3` of irregular or absent ovulation, clinical or lab signs of excess androgen (acne, hair growth, high testosterone), and polycystic-appearing ovaries on ultrasound, after excluding mimics. It is a metabolic disease, not just a period problem: insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, and, from years of unopposed estrogen, endometrial cancer risk.

### PMDD

Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is severe mood symptoms confined to the luteal phase that clear within days of flow. SSRIs, continuous or luteal-phase only, are first-line.

> **On the exam:** Irregular periods plus acne plus weight gain plus hair growth equals PCOS, and the next best step is usually a metabolic screen, not another ultrasound.
keyPoints: Secondary amenorrhea workup order: pregnancy test, then TSH and prolactin, then FSH.
PALM-COEIN splits abnormal bleeding into structural (polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy) and non-structural causes.
Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until sampling proves otherwise.
Endometriosis triad: painful periods, painful sex, infertility; laparoscopy is definitive.
PCOS = 2 of 3 Rotterdam criteria, and carries real diabetes and endometrial cancer risk.

checks.q: A 24-year-old has had no period for 4 months. What is the first test?
checks.why: Pregnancy is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea and is cheap to exclude. TSH, prolactin, and FSH all come after it.

checks.q: In PALM-COEIN, which letter stands for fibroids?
checks.why: Leiomyoma is the formal name for a fibroid. Adenomyosis is glands within the myometrium; polyps are focal endometrial overgrowths.

checks.q: A 28-year-old with PCOS asks why she needs a glucose and lipid screen when her complaint is irregular periods. The best explanation is that PCOS:
choices: Is driven by insulin resistance and raises diabetes and cardiovascular risk
Is caused by high thyroid hormone
checks.why: PCOS is a metabolic syndrome with insulin resistance at its core. It does not cause ovarian cancer, does not require insulin at diagnosis, and is not thyroid-driven.

lessons.title: Contraception: matching the method to the person
lessons.body:
## Effectiveness is about the human, not the chemistry

Every method has two numbers: **perfect use** (used exactly right every time) and **typical use** (used by real people with real lives). The gap between those two numbers is what actually decides how many pregnancies a method prevents, so methods are grouped into tiers by how much they depend on the user.

**Tier 1, under `1%` typical-use failure:** implant, intrauterine devices (IUDs), sterilization. Nothing to remember daily.

**Tier 2, roughly `4-9%`:** injection, pill, patch, ring. Perfect use is about `0.3%` for the pill, but typical use is near `7%` because people miss doses.

**Tier 3, `13-21%`:** condoms, diaphragm, withdrawal, fertility awareness.

> **Key:** The pill is not a weak method. Forgetting the pill is. Counseling that closes the perfect-typical gap, or moves the patient to a method with no gap, prevents more pregnancies than any lecture about biology.

### Combined hormonal methods (estrogen plus progestin)

Pill, patch, and vaginal ring all suppress the FSH and LH surge so no egg is released, plus they thicken cervical mucus and thin the lining. Bonuses: lighter and more predictable periods, less acne, less ovarian and endometrial cancer risk.

The risk that matters is clotting. Estrogen raises the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) and arterial events. The US Medical Eligibility Criteria (US MEC) rates conditions `1` (no restriction) to `4` (unacceptable risk, do not use). **Category 4 for estrogen** includes:

- Migraine **with aura** at any age
- Smoking and age `>= 35` (`15` or more cigarettes a day)
- Current or past VTE, or known thrombophilia
- Uncontrolled hypertension (`>= 160/100`)
- Current breast cancer
- Under `21` days postpartum
- Complicated valvular disease, lupus with antiphospholipid antibodies, or vascular complications of diabetes

> **Trap:** Migraine *without* aura is usually fine. Migraine *with* aura is a hard stop for estrogen because it multiplies stroke risk.

### Progestin-only options

When estrogen is out, progestin is almost always in. Progestin-only pills (the norethindrone type must be taken within the same `3`-hour window daily; drospirenone has a `24`-hour window), the injection (depot medroxyprogesterone, every `13` weeks, may reduce bone density reversibly and delay return of fertility up to `10` months), and the implant (etonogestrel, `3` years, the single most effective reversible method).

### IUDs

**Copper**: no hormones, `10-12` years, works by making the uterus toxic to sperm. Downside is heavier, crampier periods. It is also the most effective emergency contraception.

**Levonorgestrel**: `3-8` years depending on the device, thins the lining, often lightens or stops periods, and treats heavy bleeding as a side benefit.

### Emergency contraception, by window

1. **Copper IUD** within `5` days: over `99%` effective, and it stays as ongoing contraception. Best option.
2. **Ulipristal** `30 mg` oral within `5` days: more effective than levonorgestrel, and holds up better at higher body weight.
3. **Levonorgestrel** `1.5 mg` oral within `3` days: over the counter, no prescription, less effective after `72` hours and at higher body weight.

None of these end an established pregnancy; they delay or prevent ovulation.

> **On shift:** Start with what the patient wants, not with what you think is best. Ask about bleeding preferences, needles, partner awareness, and how quickly they might want to get pregnant, then lay the tiers next to those answers.
keyPoints: Tier 1 (implant, IUD, sterilization) has under 1% typical-use failure because it removes the user from the equation.
US MEC category 4 for estrogen: migraine with aura, smoker 35 or older, VTE history, uncontrolled hypertension, current breast cancer, under 21 days postpartum.
Progestin-only methods are the default when estrogen is contraindicated.
Copper IUD within 5 days is the most effective emergency contraception and continues as ongoing coverage.
Levonorgestrel emergency pills work within 72 hours and are less effective at higher body weight; ulipristal covers 5 days.

checks.q: A 36-year-old who smokes 20 cigarettes daily wants the combined pill. What should you tell her?
choices: Combined pills are safe if she halves her smoking
Estrogen is US MEC category 4 here; offer progestin-only or an IUD
She needs a clotting panel first, then combined pills
Combined pills are fine because she is under 40
checks.why: Smoking plus age 35 or older is category 4 for estrogen due to cardiovascular risk. Progestin-only methods and IUDs have no such restriction.

checks.q: Unprotected sex occurred 4 days ago. Which option is most effective?
choices: A combined oral contraceptive started today
checks.why: The copper IUD is over 99% effective up to 5 days and continues as contraception. Levonorgestrel drops off sharply after 72 hours.

checks.q: Which contraceptive headache is the one that forbids estrogen?
checks.why: Aura marks a substantially higher ischemic stroke risk that estrogen compounds. Migraine without aura is generally category 2 under age 35.

lessons.title: Pregnancy physiology and the prenatal schedule
lessons.body:
## Pregnancy is a whole-body event

By the third trimester the pregnant body is running a second circulation. Knowing the normal shifts keeps you from treating a normal value as a crisis, and from calling a real crisis normal.

**Blood.** Plasma volume rises `40-50%`, red cell mass only `20-30%`. The dilution makes hemoglobin drop, which is why the anemia cutoff in pregnancy is lower (roughly `11 g/dL` in the first and third trimesters). Clotting factors rise, so pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state and VTE risk goes up about `4-5` fold.

**Heart.** Cardiac output climbs `30-50%`. Heart rate rises `10-20` beats per minute. Blood pressure *falls* in the second trimester and returns to baseline near term. A systolic flow murmur is normal; a diastolic murmur is not.

**Lungs.** Progesterone drives deeper breaths, so minute ventilation rises about `40%` and carbon dioxide falls. Baseline is a mild respiratory alkalosis. Shortness of breath is common; hypoxia is not.

**Kidneys.** Glomerular filtration rises `50%`, so creatinine and blood urea nitrogen run *low*. A creatinine of `1.0` in pregnancy is abnormal.

**GI.** Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle, giving reflux, constipation, and gallstones.

> **Trap:** A pregnant trauma patient can lose `1200-1500 mL` of blood before her vital signs change, because the extra volume buffers her. Normal vitals do not mean she is fine.

### Dating the pregnancy

**Naegele rule**: first day of the LMP, minus `3` months, plus `7` days, plus `1` year. LMP of `March 10` gives a due date of `December 17`. This assumes a regular `28`-day cycle. First-trimester ultrasound (crown-rump length) is accurate to within about `5-7` days and overrides the LMP when they disagree by more than that.

### Visit schedule

- Every `4` weeks until `28` weeks
- Every `2` weeks from `28` to `36` weeks
- Weekly from `36` weeks to delivery

Every visit: blood pressure, weight, urine dip, fundal height (in centimeters it roughly equals weeks of gestation from `20-36` weeks), and fetal heart tones (`110-160` beats per minute).

### Labs and screening by timing

**First visit:** blood type and Rh with antibody screen, complete blood count, rubella and varicella immunity, hepatitis B and C, HIV, syphilis, gonorrhea and chlamydia, urine culture, cervical cytology if due.

**Aneuploidy screening:** cell-free fetal DNA from `10` weeks; nuchal translucency with first-trimester serum at `11-14` weeks; quad screen at `15-22` weeks. Diagnostic tests are chorionic villus sampling (`10-13` weeks) and amniocentesis (`15+` weeks).

**Anatomy ultrasound:** `18-22` weeks.

**Glucose screening:** `24-28` weeks (earlier if risk factors).

**Group B strep** rectovaginal culture: `36 0/7` to `37 6/7` weeks. Positive means intrapartum penicillin, not treatment now.

**Anti-D immune globulin (RhoGAM):** `28` weeks, and again within `72` hours of delivery if the newborn is Rh positive, for every Rh-negative patient.

### Prevention

Folic acid `400 mcg` daily starting before conception cuts neural tube defects; `4 mg` if there is a prior affected pregnancy. Weight gain targets run `25-35 lb` at a normal starting BMI, `28-40 lb` if underweight, `11-20 lb` if obese.

> **Key:** Teratogens to know cold: isotretinoin, warfarin, ACE inhibitors and ARBs, valproate, methotrexate, tetracyclines, lithium, and live vaccines. Alcohol has no safe amount.

> **On the exam:** Dates drive answers. `28` weeks equals RhoGAM, `24-28` equals glucose, `36-37` equals group B strep.
keyPoints: Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass, so hemoglobin falls; creatinine falls because GFR rises 50%.
Naegele rule: LMP minus 3 months, plus 7 days, plus 1 year.
Visits every 4 weeks to 28, every 2 weeks to 36, then weekly.
Timing: glucose 24-28 weeks, anti-D at 28 weeks and postpartum, group B strep 36-37 weeks.
Folic acid 400 mcg daily preconception; 4 mg with a prior neural tube defect.

checks.q: A pregnant patient at 30 weeks has a creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL. How should you read it?
choices: Normal, since creatinine rises in pregnancy
Abnormal, since GFR rises and creatinine should be lower than baseline
Normal only if she is dehydrated
checks.why: GFR rises about 50%, so normal pregnancy creatinine runs roughly 0.4-0.8. A value of 1.1 suggests real kidney impairment.

checks.q: At which gestational age is rectovaginal group B streptococcus culture collected?
checks.why: The culture is timed to stay valid through delivery. 24-28 weeks is glucose screening; 18-22 is the anatomy scan.

checks.q: LMP was June 5. Using Naegele rule, the estimated due date is:
checks.why: June 5 minus 3 months is March 5; plus 7 days is March 12 of the following year.

lessons.title: Early pregnancy emergencies and first-trimester bleeding
lessons.body:
## The one number that organizes the first trimester

After implantation the placenta makes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). In a normal early pregnancy the serum level roughly **doubles every `48` hours** through about `10` weeks. Above a threshold called the **discriminatory zone**, generally quoted as `1500-3500 mIU/mL`, a normal intrauterine pregnancy should be visible on transvaginal ultrasound.

Put those together: an hCG above the discriminatory zone with an empty uterus is an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise. An hCG that rises slowly, plateaus, or falls suggests a failing pregnancy or an ectopic.

> **Key:** Positive pregnancy test plus abdominal pain plus an empty uterus on ultrasound equals ectopic until someone proves otherwise. This is the single most tested rule in early pregnancy.

### Bleeding in the first trimester

About `25%` of pregnancies bleed early, and half of those continue normally. The differential:

- Implantation bleeding or subchorionic hematoma
- Spontaneous abortion (miscarriage)
- Ectopic pregnancy
- Molar pregnancy
- Cervical causes: polyp, infection, trauma

### The types of spontaneous abortion

| Type | Cervical os | Products passed | Key point |
|---|---|---|---|
| Threatened | Closed | None | Fetus alive, about half continue |
| Inevitable | Open | None yet | Loss is coming |
| Incomplete | Open | Some | Bleeding continues, needs evacuation |
| Complete | Closed | All | Uterus empty, bleeding settles |
| Missed | Closed | None | Fetus died, no symptoms yet |
| Septic | Open | Variable | Fever, foul discharge, a true emergency |

Management of a confirmed loss is expectant, medical (mifepristone then misoprostol), or surgical (aspiration), chosen with the patient. Septic abortion needs antibiotics and urgent evacuation.

### Ectopic pregnancy

Over `95%` implant in the fallopian tube. Risk factors are anything that scars or slows the tube: prior pelvic inflammatory disease, prior ectopic, tubal surgery, smoking, and pregnancy despite an IUD.

**Stable presentation:** `6-8` weeks of amenorrhea, one-sided pelvic pain, light bleeding, a positive test.

**Ruptured:** sudden severe pain, shoulder-tip pain from blood irritating the diaphragm, and shock signs (tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, a rigid abdomen). This is a surgical emergency. Two large-bore IVs, type and crossmatch, and the operating room.

**Methotrexate** is an option only when the patient is stable with no rupture, hCG below roughly `5000 mIU/mL`, mass under `3.5-4 cm`, no fetal cardiac activity, normal liver and kidney function, and reliable follow-up. Otherwise it is surgery (salpingostomy or salpingectomy).

> **Trap:** An IUD does not cause ectopic pregnancy. It prevents pregnancy so well that if a pregnancy happens anyway, the odds that it is ectopic go up.

### Molar pregnancy

Abnormal placental tissue overgrows with no viable fetus. Watch for a uterus larger than dates, hCG far higher than expected, severe nausea, early preeclampsia before `20` weeks, and a snowstorm or cluster-of-grapes pattern on ultrasound. Treatment is suction evacuation, then serial hCG to zero because a mole can become choriocarcinoma. Pregnancy is avoided during that surveillance window.

### Hyperemesis gravidarum

Not ordinary morning sickness: vomiting with more than `5%` body weight loss, ketones, and electrolyte derangement. Treat with IV fluids, thiamine before glucose, and antiemetics (pyridoxine with doxylamine first, then ondansetron or metoclopramide).

### Rh sensitization

An Rh-negative patient exposed to Rh-positive fetal blood makes antibodies that attack future pregnancies. Any bleeding event, trauma, procedure, or delivery in an Rh-negative patient gets **anti-D immune globulin within `72` hours**.

> **On shift:** Every reproductive-age patient with abdominal pain and syncope gets a pregnancy test on arrival, before the workup branches.
keyPoints: hCG doubles every 48 hours early; above the 1500-3500 discriminatory zone an empty uterus means ectopic until proven otherwise.
Ruptured ectopic: sudden pain, shoulder-tip pain, shock. Two large-bore IVs, crossmatch, surgery.
Methotrexate needs a stable patient, hCG under about 5000, mass under 3.5-4 cm, no cardiac activity, reliable follow-up.
Abortion type is defined by the cervical os and whether tissue has passed; septic abortion is an emergency.
Anti-D immune globulin within 72 hours of any bleeding or trauma in an Rh-negative pregnancy.

checks.q: A 27-year-old has a beta-hCG of 4200 mIU/mL, right lower quadrant pain, and a transvaginal ultrasound showing an empty uterus. What does this pattern indicate?
choices: A normal pregnancy too early to see
checks.why: Above the discriminatory zone an intrauterine pregnancy should be visible. An empty uterus with pain at that level is ectopic until proven otherwise.

checks.q: A patient has vaginal bleeding, an open cervical os, and no tissue passed at 9 weeks. This is:
checks.why: An open os with nothing passed means the loss is in progress but not complete. Threatened and missed both have a closed os.

checks.q: Which finding argues AGAINST methotrexate for an ectopic pregnancy?
choices: Systolic blood pressure of 78 with a rigid abdomen
checks.why: Hypotension with peritonitis means rupture, which requires surgery. The other findings all fit medical management criteria.

lessons.title: High blood pressure and diabetes in pregnancy
lessons.body:
## Two placental diseases

Preeclampsia and gestational diabetes both start with the placenta. In preeclampsia, the spiral arteries feeding the placenta never remodel properly, the placenta runs ischemic, and it releases factors that damage blood vessel lining throughout the body. In gestational diabetes, placental hormones make the mother insulin resistant on purpose so more glucose crosses to the fetus, and some pancreases cannot keep up.

### Sorting the hypertensive disorders

- **Chronic hypertension:** elevated before `20` weeks or before pregnancy.
- **Gestational hypertension:** new blood pressure `>= 140/90` after `20` weeks, no protein, no severe features.
- **Preeclampsia:** `>= 140/90` on two readings `4` hours apart after `20` weeks, plus proteinuria (`>= 300 mg` in 24 hours, or protein-creatinine ratio `>= 0.3`, or dipstick `2+`). Proteinuria is no longer required if severe features are present.
- **Eclampsia:** preeclampsia plus a seizure.
- **Chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia.**

**Severe features** (any one of these):

- Systolic `>= 160` or diastolic `>= 110`
- Platelets under `100,000`
- Creatinine over `1.1` or doubled
- Liver enzymes at twice the upper limit, or severe right upper quadrant pain
- Pulmonary edema
- New headache unresponsive to medication, or visual changes

> **Key:** `140/90` names the disease. `160/110` changes the plan. Severe-range pressure needs treatment within `30-60` minutes with IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or oral immediate-release nifedipine.

### Magnesium sulfate

Magnesium prevents and treats eclamptic seizures. Typical dosing is a `4-6 g` IV load over `20-30` minutes, then `1-2 g` per hour. It is not an antihypertensive.

Monitor for toxicity in this order as levels rise: **deep tendon reflexes disappear first**, then respiratory rate falls below `12`, then urine output drops, then cardiac arrest. Antidote is **calcium gluconate `1 g` IV**. Magnesium is cleared by the kidney, so falling urine output means rising levels.

> **Trap:** Absent patellar reflexes is the earliest warning sign of magnesium toxicity, not a normal finding to chart and move past.

### HELLP

**H**emolysis, **E**levated **L**iver enzymes, **L**ow **P**latelets. It may appear without dramatic blood pressures. Classic presentation is right upper quadrant or epigastric pain with nausea in the third trimester. Dangerous complications are liver hematoma and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

### The cure

Delivery of the placenta is the only cure. Timing balances fetal maturity against maternal risk: preeclampsia **without** severe features generally delivers at `37` weeks; **with** severe features, at `34` weeks, or immediately at any gestational age if the mother or fetus is unstable. Preeclampsia can still appear up to `6` weeks **after** delivery.

Prevention: low-dose aspirin `81 mg` daily starting at `12-16` weeks for high-risk patients (prior preeclampsia, chronic hypertension, diabetes, kidney disease, autoimmune disease, multiple gestation).

### Gestational diabetes

Screened at `24-28` weeks. The common two-step approach is a `50 g` oral load with a `1`-hour draw; `>= 130-140 mg/dL` (threshold varies by institution) sends the patient to a `100 g` `3`-hour confirmatory test. Two or more abnormal values on the 3-hour test confirm the diagnosis. Targets on treatment: fasting under `95`, `1`-hour post-meal under `140`, `2`-hour under `120`.

First-line management is diet and exercise. If targets are missed, **insulin** is the preferred drug in pregnancy. Risks to the fetus are macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, birth injury, and neonatal hypoglycemia after birth when the maternal glucose supply stops but the newborn's insulin is still high.

**Pregestational diabetes** is different and more dangerous: high glucose during organogenesis causes congenital heart and neural tube defects, so the target is a hemoglobin A1c under `6.5%` *before* conception. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are stopped, and a `20`-week fetal echocardiogram is added.

> **On shift:** Third-trimester epigastric pain is preeclampsia or HELLP until the pressure, platelets, and liver enzymes say otherwise. It is not reflux.
keyPoints: Preeclampsia: 140/90 twice after 20 weeks plus proteinuria, or severe features with or without protein.
Severe features include 160/110, platelets under 100,000, doubled creatinine, doubled transaminases, pulmonary edema, headache, visual changes.
Magnesium sulfate prevents seizures; reflexes go first in toxicity; calcium gluconate 1 g IV is the antidote.
Delivery is the only cure: 37 weeks without severe features, 34 weeks with them, sooner if unstable.
Gestational diabetes screened at 24-28 weeks; diet first, insulin if targets are missed; fasting goal under 95.

checks.q: A patient at 35 weeks has a blood pressure of 164/108, a headache, and platelets of 82,000. How is she classified?
checks.why: Severe-range pressure, headache, and platelets under 100,000 are each a severe feature. Gestational hypertension by definition has none.

checks.q: A patient on a magnesium infusion has absent patellar reflexes and a respiratory rate of 10. What do you do first?
choices: Stop the magnesium and give calcium gluconate 1 g IV
Give a fluid bolus and recheck in an hour
checks.why: These are magnesium toxicity signs. Stop the drug and give the antidote. Labetalol treats pressure, not magnesium levels.

checks.q: Which is the preferred medication when diet fails to control gestational diabetes?
checks.why: Insulin does not cross the placenta and is preferred. Warfarin and ACE inhibitors are teratogens and neither treats glucose.

lessons.title: The third trimester: preterm labor, membranes, bleeding, and monitoring
lessons.body:
## Time is the currency

Everything in the third trimester trades one risk against another: the risk of staying in against the risk of coming out. A baby at `26` weeks is fragile; a baby behind a bleeding placenta is in immediate danger. Your job is to recognize which clock is running.

### Preterm labor

Regular contractions with cervical change before `37` weeks. Two interventions change outcomes:

**Antenatal corticosteroids.** Betamethasone `12 mg` IM, two doses `24` hours apart (or dexamethasone `6 mg` IM every `12` hours for four doses), given from `24` to `34` weeks. Steroids mature fetal lungs and cut respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular hemorrhage, and death. Benefit peaks `24-48` hours after the first dose.

**Tocolysis** (nifedipine, indomethacin before `32` weeks, terbutaline) does not prolong pregnancy meaningfully on its own. It buys `48` hours for steroids to work and for transfer to a hospital with a neonatal ICU. That is its whole job.

Magnesium sulfate before `32` weeks is added for fetal neuroprotection against cerebral palsy.

> **Key:** Tocolysis does not save the baby. Steroids and the right nursery do. Tocolysis only buys the time to get both.

### Ruptured membranes

**PROM** is rupture before labor starts at term. **PPROM** is rupture before `37` weeks, which is the dangerous one because of infection and cord compression.

The diagnosis is a **sterile speculum** exam with three findings:

- **Pooling**: fluid collected in the posterior fornix
- **Nitrazine**: paper turns blue because amniotic fluid is alkaline (pH `7.1-7.3`) against normal vaginal acid (`3.8-4.5`)
- **Ferning**: dried fluid crystallizes into a fern pattern under the microscope

> **Trap:** No digital cervical exam once membranes are ruptured preterm. Every finger introduces bacteria and shortens the latency period. Sterile speculum only.

### Third-trimester bleeding

| | Placenta previa | Abruption | Vasa previa |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pain | Painless | Painful, constant | Painless |
| Uterus | Soft | Rigid, tender, board-like | Soft |
| Blood | Maternal, bright red | Maternal, may be concealed | **Fetal** |
| Fetal status | Usually stable | Distress common | Rapid, severe distress |
| Trigger | Spontaneous | Trauma, hypertension, cocaine | Membrane rupture |

**Never do a digital vaginal exam in third-trimester bleeding until previa is excluded by ultrasound.** A finger through a previa can cause catastrophic hemorrhage.

Abruption is a clinical diagnosis. Ultrasound misses roughly half of abruptions, so a normal scan does not rule it out.

### Growth and post-term

**Intrauterine growth restriction** is estimated fetal weight under the `10th` percentile, usually from placental insufficiency, and is followed with serial growth scans and umbilical artery Doppler. **Post-term** is `42 0/7` weeks or beyond; most practices induce by `41-42` weeks because stillbirth and meconium risk climb.

### Reading the fetal monitor

- **Baseline:** `110-160` beats per minute.
- **Variability:** the squiggle in the line, `6-25` beats per minute is moderate and is the single best sign of a well-oxygenated fetal brain.
- **Accelerations:** rises of `15` beats for `15` seconds. Reassuring.
- **Early decelerations:** mirror the contraction, nadir with the peak. Head compression. Benign.
- **Variable decelerations:** abrupt, V-shaped, unrelated to contraction timing. Cord compression. Reposition, give oxygen, consider amnioinfusion.
- **Late decelerations:** begin after the contraction peak and return to baseline after it ends. Placental insufficiency. This is the worrying one. Reposition to left side, stop oxytocin, oxygen, IV fluid, and prepare for delivery if they persist.

Memory hook: **VEAL CHOP**. Variable-Cord, Early-Head, Acceleration-OK, Late-Placenta.

### Trauma in pregnancy

After `20` weeks, lying flat lets the uterus compress the inferior vena cava and drop cardiac output by up to `30%`. Tilt the patient `15-30` degrees to the **left**, or manually displace the uterus. Resuscitate the mother fully: imaging, medication, and CPR are all done as they would be for anyone else. Add continuous fetal monitoring for at least `4` hours and anti-D immune globulin if she is Rh negative.

> **On shift:** Mother first, always. The best treatment for the fetus is a fully resuscitated mother.
keyPoints: Betamethasone 12 mg IM x2, 24 hours apart, from 24 to 34 weeks; tocolysis only buys 48 hours for it.
PPROM diagnosis is sterile speculum: pooling, nitrazine blue, ferning. No digital exam.
Previa is painless with a soft uterus; abruption is painful with a rigid uterus; vasa previa bleeds fetal blood.
No digital vaginal exam in third-trimester bleeding until ultrasound excludes previa.
VEAL CHOP: Variable-Cord, Early-Head, Acceleration-OK, Late-Placenta. Late decelerations are the worrying ones.

checks.q: A patient at 33 weeks has painless bright red bleeding and a soft, non-tender uterus. What is contraindicated?
choices: IV access and type and screen
checks.why: This picture suggests placenta previa, and a digital exam can provoke massive hemorrhage. Ultrasound comes first; monitoring and IV access are appropriate.

checks.q: Decelerations that begin after the contraction peak and recover after the contraction ends indicate:
checks.why: Late decelerations reflect placental insufficiency. Early decelerations mirror the contraction (head), variables are abrupt (cord).

checks.q: A 28-week pregnant patient is on a backboard after a crash. She becomes hypotensive. What is the first maneuver?
choices: Tilt the board 15-30 degrees to the left or manually displace the uterus
Withhold fluids to avoid fluid overload
checks.why: Supine aortocaval compression by the gravid uterus cuts venous return. Left tilt or uterine displacement restores it before anything else.

lessons.title: Labor, delivery, and the first six weeks after
lessons.body:
## What labor actually is

Labor is contractions that change the cervix. False labor (Braxton Hicks) is irregular, does not intensify, eases with rest or hydration, and leaves the cervix where it was. True labor is regular, gets closer together and stronger, radiates from back to front, and dilates and thins (effaces) the cervix.

### The stages

**First stage**, onset to full dilation at `10 cm`. The latent phase runs to about `6 cm` and can take many hours. The active phase from `6 cm` on typically progresses at least `1 cm` per hour in a first pregnancy (nullipara) and faster in later ones.

**Second stage**, full dilation to delivery of the baby. Up to `3` hours for a nullipara, `2` hours for a multipara, with an extra hour allowed if there is epidural analgesia.

**Third stage**, delivery of the placenta, normally within `30` minutes. Signs of separation are a gush of blood, cord lengthening, and the uterus rising and firming.

**Fourth stage**, the first `1-2` hours postpartum, when hemorrhage is most likely.

**Cardinal movements:** engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, external rotation (restitution), expulsion.

### Analgesia

Epidural is the most effective option; watch for maternal hypotension, which is treated with fluid and left lateral positioning. Nitrous oxide, IV opioids, and local pudendal block are alternatives. Opioids given close to delivery can depress newborn breathing.

### Cesarean

Indications include non-reassuring fetal status, arrest of labor, malpresentation (breech), placenta previa, active genital herpes lesions, and cord prolapse.

### Emergency delivery, in order

1. Support the head as it crowns. Do not pull.
2. Check for a cord around the neck; slip it over the head or, if tight, clamp and cut.
3. Suction only if there is obvious obstruction.
4. Guide the shoulders: gentle downward for the anterior, then upward for the posterior.
5. Dry, warm, stimulate. Clamp and cut the cord after `30-60` seconds if the newborn is vigorous.
6. Let the placenta come on its own. Never pull the cord.
7. Massage the fundus and put the baby to the breast; both release oxytocin and clamp the uterus down.

### Shoulder dystocia

The head delivers and retracts against the perineum (the turtle sign) because the anterior shoulder is stuck behind the pubic bone. First move is **McRoberts**: hyperflex the maternal hips onto the abdomen, which rotates the pelvis and frees the shoulder. Add **suprapubic pressure**. Never pull harder on the head and never push on the fundus.

### Cord prolapse

The cord slips past the presenting part and gets compressed. Put the mother knees-to-chest or in deep Trendelenburg, use a gloved hand to lift the presenting part off the cord and do not remove it, and go to immediate cesarean.

### Postpartum hemorrhage

Defined as `>= 1000 mL` of blood loss, or any bleeding with signs of hypovolemia (the older definitions were `500 mL` vaginal and `1000 mL` cesarean). Causes are the **four Ts**:

- **Tone**: uterine atony, the cause about `70-80%` of the time
- **Trauma**: laceration, hematoma, uterine rupture
- **Tissue**: retained placenta
- **Thrombin**: coagulopathy

Start with fundal massage and bimanual compression. Uterotonics: oxytocin `10-40` units in IV fluid first line; methylergonovine `0.2 mg` IM (avoid in hypertension); carboprost `250 mcg` IM (avoid in asthma); misoprostol `800-1000 mcg`. Tranexamic acid `1 g` IV within `3` hours reduces death.

> **Key:** Atony is most of it, and massage is free and immediate. Do it while someone else draws up the drugs.

### Postpartum problems to recognize

**Endometritis**: fever, uterine tenderness, foul lochia, usually days `2-3`. Treat with clindamycin plus gentamicin.

**Postpartum preeclampsia**: can appear up to `6` weeks after delivery. Headache and high pressure after going home is not normal.

**Mastitis**: a wedge-shaped red, hot, painful breast with fever, usually from Staphylococcus aureus. **Keep breastfeeding or pumping** and give dicloxacillin or cephalexin. A fluctuant mass means abscess and needs drainage.

**Contraception after birth**: progestin-only and IUDs can start immediately. Estrogen waits at least `21` days, and longer if breastfeeding or if VTE risk factors exist.

**Depression screening**: the postpartum blues peak at days `3-5` and resolve within `2` weeks. Depression lasting longer, or with functional impairment, is postpartum depression, screened with a validated tool at the postpartum visit. Postpartum psychosis, with confusion or thoughts of harm, is a psychiatric emergency.

> **On the exam:** Fever plus a tender uterus is endometritis. Fever plus a wedge of red breast is mastitis. Fever plus calf pain is a clot.
keyPoints: True labor changes the cervix; false labor does not.
Stages: 1 to full dilation, 2 to delivery, 3 to placenta (within 30 min), 4 is the first 1-2 hours when bleeding kills.
Shoulder dystocia: McRoberts first, then suprapubic pressure. Never fundal pressure, never traction on the head.
Postpartum hemorrhage four Ts; tone is 70-80%; massage first, then oxytocin, then second-line uterotonics.
Postpartum preeclampsia can appear up to 6 weeks after delivery.

checks.q: The head delivers, then retracts tightly against the perineum and the shoulders do not follow. What is the first maneuver?
choices: Firm downward traction on the head
checks.why: McRoberts hyperflexion rotates the pelvis and relieves most dystocias. Fundal pressure worsens impaction and traction causes brachial plexus injury.

checks.q: A woman is bleeding heavily 20 minutes after delivery. The uterus feels soft and boggy. What is the first action?
choices: Take her to the operating room for hysterectomy
Order a coagulation panel and wait
checks.why: A boggy uterus is atony, the most common cause. Massage is immediate and often effective while uterotonics are prepared.

checks.q: A breastfeeding patient has a fever of 38.8 C and a wedge of red, tender breast. What should she do about feeding?
choices: Continue breastfeeding or pumping from that breast
Stop only on the affected side for 2 weeks
checks.why: Emptying the breast is part of the treatment for mastitis. Stopping causes stasis and raises abscess risk; the milk is safe for the infant.

lessons.title: Breast problems and the cancer screening calendar
lessons.body:
## The breast is glands, ducts, and fat on a chest wall

Milk-making lobules drain through ducts to the nipple, all suspended in fat and fibrous ligaments. Lymph drains mostly to the armpit (axillary) nodes, which is why an axillary exam is part of every breast exam and why nodes matter for cancer staging.

Exam: inspect sitting with arms up and on hips, looking for asymmetry, skin dimpling, nipple retraction, and the orange-peel skin (peau d'orange) of inflammatory cancer. Then palpate all quadrants plus the tail into the axilla with the patient lying down, in a systematic pattern, and check for discharge.

### Benign conditions worth knowing

- **Fibroadenoma**: the most common mass in the teens and twenties. Firm, smooth, rubbery, freely mobile. People describe it as a marble.
- **Fibrocystic change**: diffuse lumpy, ropy tissue that gets tender and more nodular right before a period and softer after.
- **Simple cyst**: round, smooth, sometimes tender, and it changes with the cycle. Ultrasound confirms it and aspiration resolves it.
- **Duct ectasia**: dilated ducts near menopause, thick green or gray discharge, subareolar tenderness.
- **Galactorrhea**: milky discharge from both nipples unrelated to nursing. Check a pregnancy test, TSH, prolactin, and the medication list (antipsychotics, metoclopramide).

> **Trap:** Bloody or clear discharge from a **single** duct on **one** side is the worrying kind. Milky discharge from both sides is usually hormonal or a medication effect.

### The mass workup

Under `30`: **ultrasound** first, because dense young breast tissue makes mammography hard to read. Over `30`: **diagnostic mammogram plus ultrasound**. Any solid, suspicious, or persistent mass gets **core needle biopsy** regardless of imaging, because a reassuring image never outranks a suspicious lump.

### Breast cancer risk

Age is the strongest risk factor. Others: female sex, a first-degree relative with breast cancer, BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation, long lifetime estrogen exposure (early menarche, late menopause, no pregnancies, first birth after `30`), chest radiation in youth, obesity after menopause, and alcohol. BRCA1 carries roughly `55-72%` lifetime breast cancer risk and a sharply raised ovarian cancer risk; carriers start MRI screening around age `25-30`.

### Mammography, where guidelines disagree

- **USPSTF (2024):** every `2` years from `40` to `74`.
- **ACS:** option to start at `40`, annual from `45` to `54`, then every `2` years or annual.
- **ACOG:** offer at `40`, start by `50` at the latest, every `1-2` years.

The shared thread is that screening starts in the forties and the interval is a conversation about false positives versus earlier detection.

### Cervical cancer screening

Nearly all cervical cancer comes from persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, which is why the screening calendar is built around the virus, not the age of first sex.

- Under `21`: no screening at all.
- `21-29`: cytology alone every `3` years.
- `30-65`: HPV testing alone every `5` years, or co-testing every `5` years, or cytology alone every `3` years.
- Over `65`: stop, if adequate prior negative screening and no high-grade history.
- After hysterectomy for benign disease with no history of high-grade lesions: stop.

Abnormal results are managed by ASCCP risk-based guidance, which combines the current result with prior history to decide between repeat testing, colposcopy, or treatment, rather than sending every abnormal result straight to colposcopy.

**HPV vaccination** is routine at `11-12` (may start at `9`), catch-up through `26`, and shared decision-making from `27-45`. Two doses if started before `15`, three if started after.

> **Key:** Vaccinated patients still get screened. The vaccine covers most but not all oncogenic types.

### Ovarian and endometrial red flags

Ovarian cancer is quiet until late: bloating, early fullness, pelvic pressure, urinary urgency, persisting for weeks. There is no useful screening test for average-risk women, so symptoms plus a pelvic ultrasound and CA-125 are the path in.

**Postmenopausal bleeding** is the endometrial cancer flag and requires evaluation every single time: transvaginal ultrasound with an endometrial stripe over `4 mm` or any persistent bleeding leads to endometrial biopsy.

> **On the exam:** Postmenopausal bleeding equals endometrial biopsy. Bloating with early satiety for weeks equals think ovarian.
keyPoints: Breast mass under 30: ultrasound first. Over 30: mammogram plus ultrasound. Suspicious means biopsy regardless of imaging.
Unilateral single-duct bloody or clear discharge is the concerning kind; bilateral milky discharge is hormonal or drug-related.
Mammography guidelines all start in the forties and differ on interval; USPSTF says every 2 years from 40 to 74.
Cervical screening: none under 21, cytology every 3 years at 21-29, HPV-based every 5 years at 30-65.
Postmenopausal bleeding always needs endometrial evaluation.

checks.q: A 22-year-old has a 2 cm firm, smooth, freely mobile breast mass. What imaging comes first?
checks.why: Dense young breast tissue limits mammography, so ultrasound is first line under 30. The description fits fibroadenoma, but imaging still comes first.

checks.q: A healthy 24-year-old with no history asks how often she needs cervical cancer screening. The answer is:
checks.why: From 21 to 29, cytology alone every 3 years is standard. Primary HPV testing every 5 years is the 30-65 option; screening does start at 21.

checks.q: A 62-year-old, 10 years past menopause, has one episode of light vaginal bleeding. What is the next step?
choices: Reassure her that occasional spotting is normal
Repeat a pelvic exam in 6 months
Evaluate with transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial biopsy
checks.why: Any postmenopausal bleeding requires evaluation for endometrial cancer. Reassurance and delay are how early cancers get missed.

lessons.title: Vaginitis, pelvic infection, menopause, infertility, and assault care
lessons.body:
## Vaginitis: three diagnoses, three fingerprints

A healthy vagina is acidic (pH `3.8-4.5`) and dominated by lactobacilli. Most vaginitis is that balance breaking.

| | Bacterial vaginosis | Candidiasis | Trichomoniasis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Discharge | Thin, gray-white | Thick, white, clumpy | Frothy, yellow-green |
| Odor | Fishy | None | Musty |
| Itch | Mild | Intense | Moderate, irritation |
| pH | `> 4.5` | `<= 4.5` | `> 4.5` |
| Whiff test | Positive | Negative | Often positive |
| Microscopy | Clue cells | Budding yeast, pseudohyphae on KOH | Motile flagellated organisms |
| Treatment | Metronidazole `500 mg` twice daily for `7` days | Fluconazole `150 mg` once | Metronidazole `500 mg` twice daily for `7` days |

Trichomoniasis is sexually transmitted, so **partners are treated**. Bacterial vaginosis and yeast are not, so partners are not.

> **Trap:** Normal pH with intense itch and no odor is yeast. An abnormal pH sends you toward bacterial vaginosis or trichomonas, not yeast.

**Atrophic vaginitis** belongs here too: after menopause, low estrogen thins the tissue, giving dryness, burning, painful sex, and a pH above `5`. Treat with moisturizers and low-dose vaginal estrogen, which carries minimal systemic absorption.

### Pelvic inflammatory disease

Infection ascending from the cervix into the uterus, tubes, and peritoneum, usually gonorrhea, chlamydia, or vaginal flora. The diagnostic bar is deliberately **low** because untreated infection scars tubes and causes infertility and ectopic pregnancy: pelvic or lower abdominal pain plus any one of cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, or adnexal tenderness is enough to treat empirically.

Outpatient treatment is ceftriaxone `500 mg` IM once, plus doxycycline `100 mg` twice daily for `14` days, plus metronidazole `500 mg` twice daily for `14` days. Admit for pregnancy, failed outpatient therapy, inability to tolerate oral medication, severe illness, or a **tubo-ovarian abscess**, which is a walled-off pus collection needing IV antibiotics and sometimes drainage. Right upper quadrant pain from perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis) can accompany it.

### Menopause

Ovarian follicles run out, estrogen falls, and FSH climbs. **Perimenopause** is the years of erratic cycles before the end; **menopause** is diagnosed retrospectively after `12` consecutive months without a period, median age `51`. Before `40` it is called primary ovarian insufficiency and needs a workup.

Hot flashes and night sweats (vasomotor symptoms) come from a destabilized temperature set point and last a median of `7-10` years. Other changes: sleep disruption, mood shifts, genitourinary atrophy, and accelerated bone loss.

**Hormone therapy** is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms, and benefits outweigh risks for most healthy patients under `60` or within `10` years of menopause. Anyone with a uterus must get a progestin alongside estrogen, because unopposed estrogen causes endometrial cancer. Risks are VTE, stroke, and breast cancer with combined therapy beyond about `5` years. Contraindicated with prior breast or estrogen-sensitive cancer, VTE, stroke, or active liver disease. Non-hormonal options: SSRIs, SNRIs, and gabapentin.

**Osteoporosis screening** with DXA begins at age `65` for all women, or earlier if risk factors are present.

### Infertility

No pregnancy after `12` months of unprotected, regularly timed intercourse, or after `6` months if the patient is over `35`. Start the workup immediately at any age with known problems such as absent periods or prior pelvic surgery.

Basic workup, run in parallel: **semen analysis** (cheap, non-invasive, and male factor is roughly `40-50%` of cases), **ovulation confirmation** with a mid-luteal progesterone, **tubal and uterine assessment** by hysterosalpingogram, and **ovarian reserve** by anti-Mullerian hormone and day-3 FSH.

> **Key:** Order the semen analysis first. Skipping it and subjecting the female partner to invasive testing is the classic workup error.

### Sexual assault care

The patient controls the pace, the order, and what is refused. Nothing here is mandatory for them.

- A trained sexual assault nurse examiner (**SANE**) performs the exam when available.
- Evidence collection is most productive within `72-120` hours, with strict chain of custody. A patient may accept medical care and decline evidence collection, or the reverse.
- **STI prophylaxis**: ceftriaxone `500 mg` IM for gonorrhea, doxycycline `100 mg` twice daily for `7` days for chlamydia, metronidazole for trichomonas, and hepatitis B vaccination if not immune.
- **HIV post-exposure prophylaxis**: start within `72` hours, ideally within hours, and continue `28` days.
- **Emergency contraception** as described earlier.
- **Reporting**: mandatory for minors, dependent adults, and older adults everywhere. For competent adults, reporting rules vary by state, and forcing a report against the patient's wishes repeats the loss of control.

> **On shift:** Ask permission before every touch, explain before every step, and let the patient say stop. Trauma-informed care is not a soft add-on here; it is the treatment.
keyPoints: pH plus whiff plus microscopy separates bacterial vaginosis, yeast, and trichomonas; only trichomonas needs partner treatment.
PID is treated on a low diagnostic bar: pelvic pain plus cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness.
Menopause is 12 months without a period, median age 51; unopposed estrogen is never given to a patient with a uterus.
Infertility is 12 months, or 6 months if over 35; start with a semen analysis.
Assault care: HIV PEP within 72 hours for 28 days, evidence collection within 72-120 hours, patient controls the pace.

checks.q: A patient has thin gray discharge, a fishy odor, pH of 5.2, and clue cells. What is the diagnosis and does the partner need treatment?
checks.why: Clue cells with high pH and a positive whiff test are bacterial vaginosis, which is a flora imbalance, not a sexually transmitted infection, so partners are not treated.

checks.q: A 33-year-old couple has not conceived after 14 months. What is the most appropriate first test?
checks.why: Male factor accounts for 40-50% of infertility and semen analysis is cheap and non-invasive. Invasive female testing before it is the classic error.

checks.q: A patient presents 8 hours after a sexual assault. Which time-sensitive intervention must not be delayed?
choices: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis, started within 72 hours
checks.why: HIV PEP loses effectiveness after 72 hours and runs 28 days. The other options have no role in acute assault care.

cards.front: What does each letter in GTPAL stand for?
cards.back: Gravida (total pregnancies), Term (>= 37 weeks), Preterm (20 to 36 6/7 weeks), Abortions (losses before 20 weeks), Living children.

cards.front: What is a normal menstrual cycle length and flow duration?
cards.back: Cycle 24 to 38 days counted day 1 to day 1, flow 8 days or fewer. Heavy is measured in pads soaked per hour and clots larger than a quarter.

cards.front: Before any gynecologic or abdominal workup in a reproductive-age patient, what test is non-negotiable?
cards.back: A pregnancy test. Patients can be wrong about whether pregnancy is possible, and the result changes almost every downstream decision.

cards.front: What does cervical motion tenderness on bimanual exam suggest?
cards.back: Peritoneal irritation around the tubes, classically pelvic inflammatory disease. It is one of the three minimum criteria for treating PID empirically.

cards.front: In what order do you do the speculum and bimanual parts of a pelvic exam, and why?
cards.back: Speculum first, so samples are collected before lubricant and manipulation contaminate them. Bimanual second, for uterine size, tenderness, and adnexal masses.

cards.front: Is a pelvic exam required before prescribing hormonal contraception?
cards.back: No. A blood pressure and a focused history screening for contraindications are what is needed. Requiring a pelvic exam is a barrier, not a safeguard.

cards.front: What two slides make up a wet mount, and what does each show?
cards.back: Saline slide shows clue cells and motile trichomonads; potassium hydroxide slide shows budding yeast and pseudohyphae and drives the whiff test.

cards.front: What is the test order for secondary amenorrhea?
cards.back: Pregnancy test first, then TSH and prolactin, then FSH. High FSH points to the ovary; low or normal FSH points upstream to the hypothalamus or pituitary.

cards.front: How are primary and secondary amenorrhea defined?
cards.back: Primary: no period by 15 with normal breast development, or by 13 with none. Secondary: no period for 3 months, or 6 months if cycles were irregular.

cards.front: What does PALM-COEIN stand for?
cards.back: Structural: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy. Non-structural: Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not otherwise classified.

cards.front: What are the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS?
cards.back: Any 2 of 3: irregular or absent ovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, after excluding mimics like thyroid disease.

cards.front: What is the classic symptom triad of endometriosis?
cards.back: Painful periods, painful intercourse (dyspareunia), and infertility. Laparoscopy is definitive, but treatment often begins empirically with NSAIDs and hormones.

cards.front: How do fibroids and adenomyosis feel differently on exam?
cards.back: Fibroids give a firm, irregularly enlarged uterus. Adenomyosis gives a uniformly enlarged, boggy, tender uterus.

cards.front: What is first-line treatment for premenstrual dysphoric disorder?
cards.back: SSRIs, given continuously or only in the luteal phase. Symptoms are severe, confined to the luteal phase, and resolve within days of flow starting.

cards.front: Which contraceptive methods are tier 1, and what is their typical-use failure rate?
cards.back: Implant, IUDs, and sterilization, all under 1%. They are tier 1 because nothing depends on the user remembering anything.

cards.front: Why does the pill fail near 7% in typical use when perfect use is 0.3%?
cards.back: The gap is missed and late doses. The chemistry is excellent; the daily adherence is what fails, which is why counseling targets that gap.

cards.front: Name five US MEC category 4 contraindications to estrogen-containing contraception.
cards.back: Migraine with aura, smoking at age 35 or older, current or past VTE, uncontrolled hypertension at or above 160/100, current breast cancer, and under 21 days postpartum.

cards.front: How often is the contraceptive injection given, and what are its two notable drawbacks?
cards.back: Depot medroxyprogesterone every 13 weeks. Reversible bone density loss and delayed return of fertility, up to about 10 months after the last dose.

cards.front: How do the copper and levonorgestrel IUDs differ?
cards.back: Copper: hormone-free, 10 to 12 years, heavier crampier periods. Levonorgestrel: 3 to 8 years, thins the lining, lightens or stops periods, treats heavy bleeding.

cards.front: Rank the three emergency contraception options by window and effectiveness.
cards.back: Copper IUD within 5 days, over 99% effective and stays as contraception. Ulipristal 30 mg within 5 days. Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg within 3 days, weakest of the three.

cards.front: Which contraceptive method is the most effective reversible option, and for how long?
cards.back: The etonogestrel implant, effective for 3 years, with failure well under 1% because it removes user error entirely.

cards.front: What happens to creatinine in pregnancy and why?
cards.back: It falls, because glomerular filtration rate rises about 50%. Normal is roughly 0.4 to 0.8, so a creatinine of 1.0 in pregnancy signals real impairment.

cards.front: State the Naegele rule.
cards.back: Take the first day of the last menstrual period, subtract 3 months, add 7 days, add 1 year. It assumes a regular 28-day cycle.

cards.front: What is the standard prenatal visit interval schedule?
cards.back: Every 4 weeks until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks, then weekly until delivery.

cards.front: When is group B streptococcus cultured and what does a positive result mean?
cards.back: Rectovaginal culture at 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks. Positive means intrapartum IV penicillin during labor, not antibiotic treatment at the time of the culture.

cards.front: When does an Rh-negative pregnant patient receive anti-D immune globulin routinely?
cards.back: At 28 weeks, and again within 72 hours of delivery if the newborn is Rh positive. Also after any bleeding event, trauma, or invasive procedure.

cards.front: How much folic acid is recommended before conception, and when does that dose change?
cards.back: 400 mcg daily starting before conception. It rises to 4 mg daily if there was a prior pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect.

cards.front: Name six drugs that are clear teratogens.
cards.back: Isotretinoin, warfarin, ACE inhibitors and ARBs, valproate, methotrexate, tetracyclines, and lithium. Alcohol has no safe amount in pregnancy.

cards.front: How fast should beta-hCG rise in a normal early pregnancy?
cards.back: It roughly doubles every 48 hours through about 10 weeks. A slow rise, plateau, or fall suggests a failing pregnancy or an ectopic.

cards.front: What is the discriminatory zone and what does an empty uterus above it mean?
cards.back: About 1500 to 3500 mIU/mL of hCG, above which a normal intrauterine pregnancy should be visible on transvaginal ultrasound. An empty uterus means ectopic until proven otherwise.

cards.front: How do you tell threatened from inevitable from incomplete abortion?
cards.back: Threatened: os closed, nothing passed. Inevitable: os open, nothing passed yet. Incomplete: os open, some tissue passed, bleeding continues.

cards.front: What are the signs of a ruptured ectopic pregnancy?
cards.back: Sudden severe pelvic pain, shoulder-tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation by blood, a rigid abdomen, tachycardia, hypotension, and pallor. It is a surgical emergency.

cards.front: List the criteria that allow methotrexate for an ectopic pregnancy.
cards.back: Hemodynamically stable, no rupture, hCG below roughly 5000, mass under 3.5 to 4 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, normal liver and kidney function, reliable follow-up.

cards.front: What findings suggest a molar pregnancy?
cards.back: Uterus larger than dates, hCG far above expected, severe nausea, preeclampsia before 20 weeks, and a snowstorm or cluster-of-grapes ultrasound pattern.

cards.front: What separates hyperemesis gravidarum from ordinary morning sickness?
cards.back: More than 5% body weight loss, ketonuria, and electrolyte derangement. Treat with IV fluids, thiamine before glucose, and antiemetics starting with pyridoxine plus doxylamine.

cards.front: What blood pressure numbers define preeclampsia and severe range?
cards.back: 140/90 on two readings 4 hours apart after 20 weeks defines it. 160/110 is severe range and needs treatment within 30 to 60 minutes.

cards.front: List the severe features of preeclampsia.
cards.back: Systolic 160 or more or diastolic 110 or more, platelets under 100,000, creatinine over 1.1 or doubled, transaminases at twice normal or severe right upper quadrant pain, pulmonary edema, refractory headache, visual changes.

cards.front: What is the magnesium sulfate regimen for eclampsia prevention, and what order do toxicity signs appear in?
cards.back: Load 4 to 6 g IV over 20 to 30 minutes, then 1 to 2 g per hour. Toxicity: reflexes disappear first, then respiratory rate under 12, then falling urine output, then cardiac arrest.

cards.front: What is the antidote for magnesium toxicity?
cards.back: Calcium gluconate 1 g IV, along with stopping the infusion. Magnesium is renally cleared, so falling urine output predicts rising levels.

cards.front: What does HELLP stand for and how does it typically present?
cards.back: Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets. Classically right upper quadrant or epigastric pain with nausea in the third trimester, sometimes without dramatic blood pressures.

cards.front: When is delivery timed for preeclampsia with and without severe features?
cards.back: Without severe features, 37 weeks. With severe features, 34 weeks, or immediately at any gestational age if the mother or fetus becomes unstable.

cards.front: What are the glucose targets once gestational diabetes is being treated?
cards.back: Fasting under 95, 1 hour after a meal under 140, 2 hours after a meal under 120. Diet and exercise first, insulin if targets are missed.

cards.front: Who gets low-dose aspirin in pregnancy, at what dose and when?
cards.back: 81 mg daily from 12 to 16 weeks for high preeclampsia risk: prior preeclampsia, chronic hypertension, diabetes, kidney disease, autoimmune disease, or multiple gestation.

cards.front: What antenatal steroid regimen is used, at what gestational ages, and why?
cards.back: Betamethasone 12 mg IM, two doses 24 hours apart, from 24 to 34 weeks. It matures fetal lungs and reduces respiratory distress, intraventricular hemorrhage, and death.

cards.front: What is the actual purpose of tocolysis?
cards.back: To buy about 48 hours for corticosteroids to take effect and for transfer to a hospital with a neonatal ICU. It does not meaningfully prolong pregnancy by itself.

cards.front: What three speculum findings confirm ruptured membranes?
cards.back: Pooling of fluid in the posterior fornix, nitrazine paper turning blue from alkaline amniotic fluid, and ferning of dried fluid under the microscope.

cards.front: How do placenta previa and placental abruption differ clinically?
cards.back: Previa: painless bright red bleeding, soft uterus, fetus usually stable. Abruption: painful constant bleeding, rigid tender uterus, blood may be concealed, fetal distress common.

cards.front: What makes vasa previa uniquely dangerous?
cards.back: The bleeding is fetal blood, not maternal, so a small volume loss causes rapid severe fetal compromise. It classically bleeds when membranes rupture.

cards.front: What does VEAL CHOP decode to?
cards.back: Variable decelerations from Cord compression, Early from Head compression, Accelerations are OK, Late from Placental insufficiency.

cards.front: What is normal fetal heart rate baseline and moderate variability?
cards.back: Baseline 110 to 160 beats per minute. Moderate variability is 6 to 25 beats per minute and is the best single sign of adequate fetal brain oxygenation.

cards.front: Why is a pregnant trauma patient past 20 weeks tilted to the left?
cards.back: Supine, the uterus compresses the inferior vena cava and can cut cardiac output up to 30%. Tilt 15 to 30 degrees left or manually displace the uterus.

cards.front: How do you tell true labor from false labor?
cards.back: True labor has regular contractions that intensify and produce cervical dilation and effacement. False labor is irregular, does not progress, eases with rest, and leaves the cervix unchanged.

cards.front: What are the four stages of labor?
cards.back: First: onset to 10 cm. Second: full dilation to delivery of the baby. Third: delivery of the placenta, normally within 30 minutes. Fourth: the first 1 to 2 hours postpartum.

cards.front: What is the first maneuver for shoulder dystocia, and what two actions are forbidden?
cards.back: McRoberts: hyperflex the hips onto the abdomen, then add suprapubic pressure. Never apply fundal pressure and never pull harder on the fetal head.

cards.front: How is umbilical cord prolapse managed until cesarean?
cards.back: Knees-to-chest or deep Trendelenburg, and a gloved hand elevating the presenting part off the cord, left in place during transport to immediate cesarean.

cards.front: What are the four Ts of postpartum hemorrhage and which is most common?
cards.back: Tone (uterine atony, 70 to 80% of cases), Trauma, Tissue (retained placenta), Thrombin (coagulopathy). Massage the fundus first while drugs are prepared.

cards.front: Name the uterotonics for postpartum hemorrhage and the condition each one avoids.
cards.back: Oxytocin 10 to 40 units IV first. Methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM, avoid in hypertension. Carboprost 250 mcg IM, avoid in asthma. Misoprostol 800 to 1000 mcg. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours.

cards.front: How do postpartum blues, depression, and psychosis differ?
cards.back: Blues peak at days 3 to 5 and clear within 2 weeks. Depression persists beyond that or impairs function. Psychosis brings confusion or thoughts of harm and is a psychiatric emergency.

cards.front: What imaging comes first for a breast mass under age 30 versus over 30?
cards.back: Under 30: ultrasound, because dense tissue obscures mammography. Over 30: diagnostic mammogram plus ultrasound. Suspicious masses get core needle biopsy either way.

cards.front: Which nipple discharge pattern is concerning and which is usually benign?
cards.back: Concerning: bloody or clear, from one duct, on one side. Usually benign: milky discharge from both nipples, which points to pregnancy, thyroid disease, prolactinoma, or medication.

cards.front: What is the cervical cancer screening calendar from 21 to over 65?
cards.back: No screening under 21. Age 21 to 29: cytology every 3 years. Age 30 to 65: HPV alone or co-testing every 5 years, or cytology every 3 years. Over 65: stop if prior screening was adequate and negative.

cards.front: What describes a fibroadenoma on exam and who gets them?
cards.back: Firm, smooth, rubbery, freely mobile, often described as a marble. It is the most common breast mass in the teens and twenties.

cards.front: What symptoms should make you think ovarian cancer, and why is it caught late?
cards.back: Bloating, early fullness, pelvic pressure, and urinary urgency persisting for weeks. There is no effective screening test for average-risk patients, so symptoms are the entry point.

cards.front: How do vaginal pH and whiff test separate the three main causes of vaginitis?
cards.back: Bacterial vaginosis: pH above 4.5, whiff positive, clue cells. Candidiasis: pH 4.5 or below, whiff negative, pseudohyphae. Trichomoniasis: pH above 4.5, motile organisms.

cards.front: Which vaginitis requires partner treatment, and what is the regimen?
cards.back: Trichomoniasis, because it is sexually transmitted. Metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days for both partners. Bacterial vaginosis and yeast do not need partner treatment.

cards.front: What is the minimum diagnostic bar for treating pelvic inflammatory disease, and why is it set low?
cards.back: Pelvic or lower abdominal pain plus cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness. The bar is low because untreated PID scars tubes, causing infertility and ectopic pregnancy.

cards.front: How is menopause defined, and what is the median age?
cards.back: Twelve consecutive months without a period, diagnosed retrospectively, median age 51. Before age 40 it is primary ovarian insufficiency and requires a workup.

cards.front: Why must a patient with a uterus never receive estrogen alone as hormone therapy?
cards.back: Unopposed estrogen drives endometrial hyperplasia and cancer. A progestin is added to protect the lining. After hysterectomy, estrogen alone is acceptable.

cards.front: How is infertility defined, and what is the first test?
cards.back: No pregnancy after 12 months of unprotected timed intercourse, or 6 months if over 35. Start with a semen analysis: male factor is 40 to 50% of cases and the test is cheap.

cards.front: What are the time windows in sexual assault care?
cards.back: Evidence collection is most productive within 72 to 120 hours. HIV post-exposure prophylaxis starts within 72 hours and runs 28 days. Emergency contraception windows are 3 to 5 days.

quiz.q: A 26-year-old reports her last period was 7 weeks ago. She has had three pregnancies: one delivery at 38 weeks, one at 34 weeks, and one loss at 11 weeks. Both children are alive. Including the current pregnancy, what is her GTPAL?
quiz.why: The current pregnancy counts toward gravidity, giving G4. One term, one preterm, one loss before 20 weeks, two living children. G3 forgets the current pregnancy.

quiz.q: Which statement about chaperones during a pelvic exam is correct?
choices: They are needed only when the clinician is male
They should be offered and the offer documented regardless of clinician gender
They are required only for patients under 18
They replace the need for verbal consent
quiz.why: Standard practice is to offer a chaperone for every sensitive exam and document it. Gender and age do not change the offer, and a chaperone never substitutes for consent.

quiz.q: A 23-year-old with amenorrhea for 5 months has a negative pregnancy test. Which pair of tests comes next?
quiz.why: After excluding pregnancy, thyroid disease and hyperprolactinemia are the common treatable causes. Androgens and imaging come later if the initial screen is unrevealing.

quiz.q: A 42-year-old has heavy periods and a firm, irregularly enlarged uterus on bimanual exam. Which PALM-COEIN category best fits?
quiz.why: An irregularly enlarged firm uterus is classic for fibroids. Coagulopathy and ovulatory dysfunction do not change uterine contour, and iatrogenic implies a drug or device.

quiz.q: A 29-year-old with PCOS has had two periods in the past year. Beyond fertility, what is the main reason to induce regular withdrawal bleeding or use a progestin?
choices: To prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer from unopposed estrogen
quiz.why: Chronic anovulation leaves the lining under estrogen with no progesterone, driving hyperplasia. Prolactin, torsion, and iron overload are unrelated to this mechanism.

quiz.q: A 16-year-old has severe cramping on the first two days of every period since menarche at 13. Exam and ultrasound are normal. What is the best initial treatment?
choices: NSAIDs started a day or two before flow, with hormonal contraception if needed
quiz.why: This is primary dysmenorrhea, driven by prostaglandins, and NSAIDs plus hormonal suppression are first line. Surgery and GnRH agonists are far too aggressive for an initial approach.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a US MEC category 4 condition for combined hormonal contraception?
quiz.why: Prior VTE is an absolute contraindication to estrogen. Controlled hypertension, nonsmoking age 38, and aura-free migraine under 35 are all acceptable categories.

quiz.q: A patient presents 96 hours after unprotected sex and wants the most effective option that also provides ongoing contraception. What do you offer?
quiz.why: The copper IUD is over 99% effective up to 5 days and continues as contraception. Ulipristal works in the window but does not provide ongoing coverage; levonorgestrel is weak past 72 hours.

quiz.q: Which contraceptive is associated with reversible bone mineral density loss and a delayed return of fertility?
quiz.why: The injection suppresses estradiol enough to affect bone density reversibly and fertility can take up to 10 months to return. The implant, IUD, and ring do not share these effects.

quiz.q: A pregnant patient at 32 weeks has a heart rate of 96, a soft systolic murmur, and mild shortness of breath climbing stairs. How do you interpret these findings?
choices: Likely heart failure requiring echocardiography today
quiz.why: Heart rate rises 10 to 20, cardiac output rises 30 to 50% producing a flow murmur, and progesterone-driven hyperventilation causes breathlessness. A diastolic murmur or true hypoxia would change this.

quiz.q: At what gestational age is the fetal anatomy ultrasound performed?
quiz.why: The anatomy scan is done at 18 to 22 weeks. 10 to 13 weeks is chorionic villus sampling, 24 to 28 is glucose screening, 36 to 37 is group B strep.

quiz.q: An Rh-negative patient at 15 weeks has vaginal bleeding after a fall. Beyond evaluating the bleeding, what must be given?
quiz.why: Any bleeding or trauma in an Rh-negative pregnancy risks sensitization and needs anti-D within 72 hours. Steroids, magnesium, and penicillin address unrelated problems at other gestational ages.

quiz.q: A 25-year-old with a positive pregnancy test has left lower quadrant pain and light bleeding. Serum hCG is 2900 mIU/mL and transvaginal ultrasound shows no intrauterine gestational sac. She is stable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
quiz.why: hCG above the discriminatory zone with an empty uterus and unilateral pain is ectopic until proven otherwise. Threatened abortion would show an intrauterine sac.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old at 7 weeks arrives pale, with a blood pressure of 76/44, heart rate 132, severe abdominal pain, and shoulder pain. What is the immediate priority?
choices: Obtain a serial hCG in 48 hours
Two large-bore IVs, type and crossmatch, and emergent surgical consultation
quiz.why: This is a ruptured ectopic with hemorrhagic shock. Resuscitation and surgery are the answer. Serial hCG and methotrexate both require a stable patient.

quiz.q: A patient at 8 weeks has cramping and bleeding. The cervical os is closed, ultrasound shows a live embryo with cardiac activity. This is:
quiz.why: A closed os with a living embryo is a threatened abortion, and about half continue normally. Missed abortion means fetal demise with a closed os; inevitable means an open os.

quiz.q: A patient at 16 weeks has a uterus measuring at 24 weeks, an hCG of 240,000, severe vomiting, and a blood pressure of 158/98. Ultrasound shows a snowstorm pattern. Beyond evacuation, what does follow-up require?
choices: Serial hCG to zero with contraception during surveillance
No follow-up once the uterus is empty
quiz.why: Molar tissue can progress to choriocarcinoma, so hCG is tracked to zero and pregnancy is avoided so a rising hCG is interpretable. Hysterectomy is not routine.
