quiz.q: A patient at 24 weeks has vomited for 3 weeks, lost 7% of her body weight, and has ketonuria and a potassium of 3.0. What is the diagnosis and initial treatment?
choices: Hyperemesis gravidarum; IV fluids, thiamine before glucose, and antiemetics
Normal morning sickness; reassurance and crackers
quiz.why: Weight loss above 5% with ketones and electrolyte derangement defines hyperemesis. Thiamine precedes glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy.

quiz.q: A patient at 24 weeks is newly found to have a blood pressure of 146/92 on two readings 6 hours apart, with no proteinuria and normal labs. How is she classified?
quiz.why: New hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria or severe features is gestational hypertension. Chronic hypertension appears before 20 weeks; eclampsia requires a seizure.

quiz.q: Which agent is appropriate for acute treatment of a blood pressure of 172/114 in pregnancy?
quiz.why: IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or oral immediate-release nifedipine treat severe-range pressure within 30 to 60 minutes. Magnesium prevents seizures but does not lower pressure, and ACE inhibitors are teratogenic.

quiz.q: A patient at 36 weeks has epigastric pain, nausea, platelets of 74,000, AST of 210, and evidence of hemolysis on smear. Her blood pressure is 138/86. What is the diagnosis?
quiz.why: Hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets define HELLP, which can occur without severe-range pressures. Reflux and cholecystitis do not cause thrombocytopenia and hemolysis.

quiz.q: A patient with preeclampsia without severe features is now 37 weeks. What is the recommended management?
choices: Start magnesium and continue the pregnancy 3 more weeks
Discharge with weekly visits until 41 weeks
quiz.why: Delivery of the placenta is the only cure and 37 weeks is the recommended timing without severe features. Prolonging the pregnancy adds maternal risk without fetal benefit.

quiz.q: A patient at 26 weeks screens positive on a 1-hour 50 g glucose load. What is the next step?
choices: Diagnose gestational diabetes and begin diet therapy
Perform a 3-hour 100 g oral glucose tolerance test
quiz.why: The 1-hour test is a screen, not a diagnosis. Two or more abnormal values on the confirmatory 3-hour test establish gestational diabetes before any treatment begins.

quiz.q: Why do infants of mothers with poorly controlled gestational diabetes become hypoglycemic after birth?
choices: Their livers cannot store any glycogen
Maternal insulin crosses the placenta and persists in the newborn
They are born with adrenal insufficiency
Their pancreases have been making extra insulin in response to high maternal glucose, which stops abruptly at delivery
quiz.why: Fetal hyperinsulinemia continues after the maternal glucose supply is cut at cord clamping. Maternal insulin does not cross the placenta, which is why insulin is the drug of choice in pregnancy.

quiz.q: A patient at 29 weeks is in preterm labor and receives nifedipine. What is the primary purpose of this medication?
choices: To mature the fetal lungs directly
To delay delivery about 48 hours so steroids can take effect and transfer can occur
quiz.why: Tocolysis does not meaningfully prolong pregnancy or improve neonatal outcome on its own. Betamethasone matures lungs; magnesium provides neuroprotection before 32 weeks.

quiz.q: A patient at 34 weeks with a cocaine history presents with constant abdominal pain, dark vaginal bleeding, and a rigid, exquisitely tender uterus. Ultrasound is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
quiz.why: Painful bleeding with a rigid tender uterus is abruption, and ultrasound misses roughly half of them, so a normal scan does not exclude it. Previa is painless with a soft uterus.

quiz.q: The fetal monitor shows repeated decelerations that begin after the peak of each contraction and return to baseline after the contraction ends. What is the first action?
choices: Reassure the patient; this is a normal pattern
Increase the oxytocin infusion to speed delivery
Reposition to the left side, stop oxytocin, give oxygen and IV fluid
Perform an immediate digital exam to rupture membranes
quiz.why: Late decelerations indicate uteroplacental insufficiency. Intrauterine resuscitation comes first, and delivery follows if the pattern persists. Increasing oxytocin worsens the insult.

quiz.q: Moderate fetal heart rate variability is defined as:
choices: 6 to 25 beats per minute of fluctuation
Baseline of 110 to 160 beats per minute
quiz.why: Variability is the beat-to-beat fluctuation amplitude, and 6 to 25 is moderate. Baseline, accelerations, and decelerations are separate descriptors on the strip.

quiz.q: A nulliparous patient has been fully dilated and pushing for 2 hours with an epidural. The fetal heart tracing is reassuring and descent is occurring. What is appropriate?
choices: Immediate cesarean for arrest of descent
Continue pushing, since up to 4 hours is acceptable for a nullipara with an epidural
quiz.why: Second stage may last 3 hours in a nullipara, with an extra hour allowed for epidural analgesia. With reassuring tracing and ongoing descent there is no indication to intervene.

quiz.q: During delivery the head emerges and immediately retracts against the perineum. The shoulders do not deliver with gentle downward traction. What is the next action?
choices: Apply fundal pressure while an assistant pulls the head
Hyperflex the maternal hips onto the abdomen and apply suprapubic pressure
Cut the cord and prepare for cesarean
Wait for the next contraction without intervening
quiz.why: McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves most shoulder dystocias. Fundal pressure drives the shoulder harder into the pubic bone, and the head is already out so cesarean is not the path.

quiz.q: A patient with chronic hypertension has postpartum hemorrhage from atony that has not responded to massage and oxytocin. Which uterotonic should be avoided in her?
quiz.why: Methylergonovine causes vasoconstriction and can provoke hypertensive crisis. Carboprost is avoided in asthma, not hypertension; misoprostol and tranexamic acid have no such restriction here.

quiz.q: A patient is 5 days postpartum with a fever of 38.9 C, lower abdominal pain, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling lochia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
quiz.why: Fever with uterine tenderness and foul lochia is endometritis, treated with clindamycin and gentamicin. Mastitis localizes to the breast, pyelonephritis to the flank, DVT to the leg.

quiz.q: A patient calls 12 days after delivery with a severe headache and a home blood pressure of 168/106. What should you tell her?
choices: This is normal after delivery and will resolve
Take acetaminophen and call in a week
Come in now; postpartum preeclampsia can occur up to 6 weeks after delivery
quiz.why: Preeclampsia can present up to 6 weeks postpartum and severe-range pressure with headache needs urgent evaluation and treatment. Delay risks seizure and stroke.

quiz.q: A 34-year-old has a 1.5 cm firm breast mass. Diagnostic mammogram and ultrasound are both read as probably benign, but the mass is palpable and persistent. What is the next step?
choices: Reassure and repeat imaging in 1 year
Start an oral contraceptive and reassess
quiz.why: A persistent palpable mass is biopsied regardless of reassuring imaging, because imaging has a real false negative rate. Waiting a year risks missing an early cancer.

quiz.q: A 34-year-old who received the HPV vaccine at 13 asks whether she still needs cervical cancer screening.
choices: No, screening is only for unvaccinated patients
Yes, because the vaccine does not cover every oncogenic HPV type
quiz.why: The vaccine prevents most but not all oncogenic types, so the screening calendar is unchanged. At her age that means HPV-based testing every 5 years or cytology every 3 years.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old has intense vulvar itching, thick white clumpy discharge, no odor, and a vaginal pH of 4.2. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
choices: Bacterial vaginosis; metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days
Trichomoniasis; metronidazole for the patient and partner
quiz.why: Normal pH with intense itch and no odor is yeast. Bacterial vaginosis and trichomonas both raise pH above 4.5, and atrophic vaginitis occurs with low estrogen, not at 24.

quiz.q: A 21-year-old has lower abdominal pain, and exam reveals cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness. Her temperature is 37.9 C and she is tolerating fluids. What should you do?
choices: Wait for gonorrhea and chlamydia results before treating
Treat empirically with ceftriaxone IM plus doxycycline and metronidazole
Admit for intravenous antibiotics in all cases
quiz.why: The PID threshold is deliberately low because delay causes tubal scarring and infertility. Waiting for cultures wastes days, and outpatient therapy is appropriate for mild to moderate disease.

quiz.q: A 53-year-old with a uterus has disabling hot flashes and no contraindications to hormone therapy. What regimen is appropriate?
choices: Estrogen alone, at the lowest effective dose
A progestin alone, which is equally effective for hot flashes
No treatment; hormone therapy is contraindicated after age 50
quiz.why: Anyone with a uterus needs a progestin to prevent endometrial hyperplasia from unopposed estrogen. Benefits outweigh risks under 60 or within 10 years of menopause.

scenarios.title: ED: 24-year-old with abdominal pain and near-syncope
scenarios.intro: It is 2100 in a community emergency department. Triage sends back a 24-year-old who felt faint at work and has had worsening left lower abdominal pain since this morning. She walked in on her own, but she is pale and quiet. Her last period, she thinks, was about seven weeks ago, though she says her cycles are 'always weird.' She tells you she cannot be pregnant.

steps.prompt: She is on the stretcher. Pain is a 7 out of 10, left lower quadrant, sharp, worse when she moves. She had a small amount of dark vaginal spotting this afternoon. What is your first move?

choices.text: Order a urine pregnancy test and place IV access while completing the history
choices.feedback: Correct. In any reproductive-age patient with abdominal pain, the pregnancy test comes first because it splits the differential in half. Patients are frequently wrong about whether pregnancy is possible.

choices.text: Accept her statement that she cannot be pregnant and work up appendicitis and ovarian torsion
choices.feedback: Dangerous shortcut. Patient report is not a pregnancy test. Missing an ectopic because you believed the history is one of the classic malpractice patterns in emergency medicine.

choices.text: Send her for a CT of the abdomen and pelvis before any other testing
choices.feedback: Premature, and it irradiates a possibly pregnant patient. A urine pregnancy test takes two minutes and decides whether CT is even the right study.

choices.text: Give oral analgesia and reassess in an hour before any testing
choices.feedback: Pain control is reasonable, but delaying the pregnancy test for an hour in a patient with pain and spotting risks missing a time-critical diagnosis.

steps.prompt: The urine pregnancy test is positive. She is visibly surprised. Quantitative serum hCG returns at 3100 mIU/mL. Blood type is O negative. What do you order next?

choices.text: Transvaginal ultrasound to locate the pregnancy
choices.feedback: Right. Her hCG is above the discriminatory zone of roughly 1500 to 3500, so a normal intrauterine pregnancy should be visible. Where the pregnancy is located is now the entire question.

choices.text: Repeat the hCG in 48 hours and discharge her home now
choices.feedback: Serial hCG is for patients below the discriminatory zone with no pain and stable vitals. She has pain, tachycardia, and a level above the zone. She cannot go home yet.

choices.text: Start methotrexate empirically for presumed ectopic
choices.feedback: Far too early. Methotrexate requires a confirmed, unruptured ectopic in a stable patient. Giving it blindly could terminate a viable intrauterine pregnancy.

choices.text: Order a complete blood count and type and crossmatch alongside the ultrasound
choices.feedback: Reasonable and useful preparation, and her O negative status also flags the anti-D question. But the ultrasound is the study that answers the question.

steps.prompt: Ultrasound shows an empty uterus, a 3 cm left adnexal mass, and a moderate amount of free fluid in the pelvis. While the tech is finishing, she says the pain suddenly got much worse and her right shoulder now hurts.

choices.text: Activate for a ruptured ectopic: second large-bore IV, crystalloid, emergency release blood, and call obstetrics and gynecology for the operating room
choices.feedback: Correct. Shoulder pain here is blood irritating the diaphragm. With free fluid, hypotension, and tachycardia, this is a ruptured ectopic with hemorrhagic shock. Resuscitate and get to surgery.

choices.text: Give morphine for the pain and recheck the pressure in 20 minutes
choices.feedback: Treating the symptom while she bleeds internally. The shoulder pain and hypotension together are the rupture signal, not a pain control problem.

choices.text: Order a CT angiogram of the chest to evaluate the shoulder pain for pulmonary embolism
choices.feedback: The wrong diagnosis and the wrong delay. Referred shoulder pain with pelvic free fluid and hypotension is hemoperitoneum. CT wastes the minutes she does not have.

choices.text: Place her flat, open fluids wide, and call for help while you recheck the pressure
choices.feedback: The resuscitation instinct is right and buys a little time, but this needs the surgical activation and blood products called in the same breath, not after a recheck.

steps.prompt: Two units of uncrossmatched blood are running and the OR is being opened. The gynecology resident is at the bedside. Her pressure is 96/58 on transfusion. Before she leaves the department, what else does her Rh-negative blood type require you to address?

choices.text: Ensure anti-D immune globulin is ordered, since she is Rh negative with a bleeding pregnancy event
choices.feedback: Correct. Any bleeding event in an Rh-negative pregnancy risks sensitization that would endanger future pregnancies. Anti-D is given within 72 hours and is easy to forget in a resuscitation.

choices.text: Nothing; Rh status only matters at 28 weeks and at delivery
choices.feedback: Incorrect. Routine dosing happens at 28 weeks and postpartum, but any bleeding, trauma, procedure, or ectopic also requires it.

choices.text: Order anti-D but hold it until after the pathology confirms an ectopic
choices.feedback: Unnecessary delay. The indication is a bleeding pregnancy event in an Rh-negative patient, which is already established.

choices.text: Document her Rh status for the operative note and let the surgical team decide
choices.feedback: Documentation is good, but handing off a time-sensitive medication decision without naming it is how it gets missed in transitions of care.

steps.prompt: She is in the operating room for a laparoscopic salpingectomy. Her family is in the waiting room and asks you what happened. Her partner asks whether anything she did caused this.

choices.text: Explain in plain words that the pregnancy implanted in the tube instead of the uterus, that the tube ruptured and bled, and that nothing she did caused it
choices.feedback: Right on both the content and the tone. Plain language, an honest mechanism, and explicit removal of blame. Ectopic pregnancy is not caused by anything the patient did that evening.

choices.text: Tell them you cannot discuss anything and walk away
choices.feedback: Privacy rules matter, but this is avoidance rather than protection. Confirm who is authorized, then communicate. Silence in a crisis reads as bad news and erodes trust.

choices.text: Say the ectopic was probably caused by a prior sexually transmitted infection
choices.feedback: Speculative, unhelpful, and assigns blame in front of family. Prior infection is a risk factor, not a confirmed cause here, and it is not yours to disclose to a waiting room.

choices.text: Give a technical explanation using the terms hemoperitoneum, salpingectomy, and hCG discriminatory zone
choices.feedback: Accurate but unusable. Families under stress need the mechanism in plain words first. The technical terms belong in the chart.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: positive pregnancy test plus abdominal pain plus an empty uterus above the discriminatory zone equals ectopic until proven otherwise. Three things drove this case. First, the pregnancy test came before the differential, despite the patient saying she could not be pregnant. Second, referred shoulder pain with pelvic free fluid and falling pressure meant rupture and hemoperitoneum, not a musculoskeletal complaint. Third, the small item that is easiest to lose in a resuscitation, anti-D immune globulin for an Rh-negative patient, protects every pregnancy she has after this one.

scenarios.title: Classroom: a headache at 34 weeks
scenarios.intro: Work this one as a reasoning exercise. A 31-year-old at 34 weeks by a first-trimester ultrasound calls the office. She is G1 P0 with an uncomplicated pregnancy until now. For two days she has had a headache that ibuprofen and acetaminophen have not touched, and this morning she saw 'sparkles' in her vision while making breakfast. She mentions her rings are tight and she gained six pounds since last week's visit.

steps.prompt: You are on the phone with her. What do you tell her to do, and what is your leading concern?

choices.text: Have her come in now for evaluation, concerned for preeclampsia with severe features
choices.feedback: Correct. Refractory headache plus visual changes after 20 weeks is preeclampsia with severe features until proven otherwise. Rapid weight gain and edema support it but are not diagnostic on their own.

choices.text: Advise rest, hydration, and a follow-up at her scheduled visit in one week
choices.feedback: This is the missed-diagnosis pathway. A headache that does not respond to analgesics plus visual disturbance in the third trimester is never a wait-a-week problem.

choices.text: Tell her the swelling and weight gain are normal in the third trimester and reassure her
choices.feedback: Edema and weight gain alone are common, which is exactly why they are not the point. The headache and visual symptoms are the severe features driving this call.

choices.text: Ask her to check her blood pressure at a pharmacy and call back with the number
choices.feedback: The number is useful but the delay is not. With visual symptoms she needs evaluation regardless of what a pharmacy cuff reads, and a normal reading might falsely reassure her.

steps.prompt: She arrives 40 minutes later. Blood pressure is 168/112, repeated at 164/108 fifteen minutes later. She has 3+ pitting edema and brisk reflexes. Urine dipstick shows 3+ protein. What laboratory studies do you want?

choices.text: Complete blood count with platelets, creatinine, liver enzymes, and a protein-creatinine ratio
choices.feedback: Exactly the severe-feature panel. Platelets under 100,000, creatinine over 1.1 or doubled, and transaminases at twice normal each independently define severe disease and change management.

choices.text: Thyroid function tests and a lipid panel
choices.feedback: Not relevant here. These do not evaluate preeclampsia and delay the studies that decide whether she delivers today.

choices.text: Only a 24-hour urine collection, since that is the gold standard for proteinuria
choices.feedback: She already has severe-range blood pressure and neurologic symptoms, so proteinuria is no longer required for the diagnosis. Waiting 24 hours for a number you do not need is dangerous.

choices.text: A head CT to rule out other causes of headache first
choices.feedback: Imaging has a role in atypical or focal presentations, but here the severe-range pressure with visual symptoms already explains the headache. Labs and treatment come first.

steps.prompt: Platelets are 88,000, AST is 96, creatinine is 1.2, and the protein-creatinine ratio is 1.8. Her blood pressure is still 166/110 and she says the headache is worse. Name the two medication decisions that need to happen now.

choices.text: Antihypertensive for severe-range pressure within 30 to 60 minutes, plus magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis
choices.feedback: Correct, and the two serve different purposes. IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or oral immediate-release nifedipine lowers the pressure. Magnesium prevents eclamptic seizures and does nothing for blood pressure.

choices.text: Magnesium sulfate alone, since it will bring the blood pressure down as well
choices.feedback: A common misconception. Magnesium is an anticonvulsant, not an antihypertensive. Leaving 166/110 untreated leaves stroke risk untouched.

choices.text: Start oral lisinopril to protect her kidneys given the rising creatinine
choices.feedback: ACE inhibitors are teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy. They also act far too slowly for severe-range pressure.

choices.text: Antihypertensive now, and hold magnesium unless she actually seizes
choices.feedback: Half right. Treating the pressure is correct, but magnesium is given prophylactically in severe preeclampsia. Waiting for the seizure means you have already lost the prevention window.

steps.prompt: Two hours into the magnesium infusion the nurse reports that patellar reflexes can no longer be elicited, the respiratory rate is 11, and urine output over the last hour was 18 mL. What is happening and what do you do?

choices.text: Magnesium toxicity: stop the infusion and give calcium gluconate 1 g IV
choices.feedback: Correct, and the sequence of signs is the teaching point. Reflexes go first, then respiratory depression, then oliguria. Low urine output also means she is clearing the drug poorly, so levels keep climbing.

choices.text: Increase the magnesium rate, since a lower blood pressure means it is working
choices.feedback: This is the fatal version of the misconception. Magnesium does not treat blood pressure, and pushing more into a patient with absent reflexes and a respiratory rate of 11 heads toward respiratory and cardiac arrest.

choices.text: Give a fluid bolus to improve urine output and continue the magnesium unchanged
choices.feedback: Fluids need caution in preeclampsia because of pulmonary edema risk, and continuing the infusion in the face of toxicity signs is the core error. Stop the drug first.

choices.text: Stop the magnesium and observe closely without giving anything else
choices.feedback: Stopping is the right instinct and half the answer. With a respiratory rate already at 11, calcium gluconate is given rather than waiting to see how far it falls.

steps.prompt: She stabilizes after calcium gluconate, and magnesium is restarted at a lower rate with close monitoring. She asks how long she can stay pregnant, because 34 weeks feels early to her. What is the honest answer?

choices.text: Delivery is the only cure, and with severe features at 34 weeks the recommendation is to deliver now after steroids are considered
choices.feedback: Correct and honest. Preeclampsia with severe features delivers at 34 weeks, or immediately at any gestation if mother or fetus becomes unstable. Betamethasone is given if it will not delay a necessary delivery.

choices.text: With magnesium and blood pressure medication she can safely continue to 39 weeks
choices.feedback: False reassurance. Those medications manage the disease; they do not treat it. Only delivery of the placenta cures preeclampsia.

choices.text: Tell her the decision belongs to the obstetrician and you cannot comment
choices.feedback: Deflection where a clear answer is available. Patients facing early delivery deserve to understand the reasoning, even when another clinician signs the order.

choices.text: Explain that once the baby is delivered she is completely out of danger
choices.feedback: Incorrect and potentially harmful. Preeclampsia and eclampsia can occur up to 6 weeks postpartum, so she needs blood pressure follow-up and clear return precautions after discharge.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: after 20 weeks, a headache that analgesics do not touch plus visual changes is preeclampsia until the blood pressure, platelets, creatinine, and liver enzymes say otherwise. Four ideas carry forward. 140/90 names the disease and 160/110 demands treatment within 30 to 60 minutes. Antihypertensives and magnesium do different jobs and neither substitutes for the other. Magnesium toxicity announces itself in order, reflexes then respirations then urine output, with calcium gluconate 1 g IV as the antidote. And delivery is the only cure, which is why the timing conversation is about 34 versus 37 weeks rather than about riding it out, with preeclampsia still possible for 6 weeks after she goes home.
